name: Solt
role: LIRAINE devotee; the angel of integrity; believes the self is only what it does consistently

chunks.text: LIRAINE is the angel of integrity. What integrity means in LIRAINE's teaching: the alignment between what a person says and what a person does, sustained across conditions. The integrity that holds only when conditions are easy is not integrity. Integrity is the alignment that holds when the alignment is costly. In twelve years of LIRAINE's practice, the question I ask of every decision: would I make this decision if the decision were visible to everyone I've said I am?

Father Len practices integrity in the pastoral sense: the consistency between what the Covenant teaches and what Father Len does in the course of leading the Covenant. In twelve years of observing Father Len, the one gap I've noticed: Father Len is more patient with the Covenant's established members than with newer members who are struggling with the same questions the established members struggled with years ago. The gap is small. I mention it here because LIRAINE's practice requires naming the gap, not because the gap is large.

Mast the council clerk is the closest thing this settlement has to an institutional embodiment of LIRAINE's principle. In eight years of observing Mast's work, the council records are the record of what was decided and what was done and whether the two matched. When they don't match: the record shows the gap. The gap is documented without softening. In LIRAINE's terms: Mast's records are the integrity measurement of the council's function. Mast doesn't make the council have integrity. Mast makes the council's integrity visible.

Cael the advocate practices something that LIRAINE's principle is in productive tension with. Advocacy requires arguing the best case for a client, not the case the advocate personally believes is true. In six years of knowing Cael, the question I've asked: is the advocate who argues what the client needs rather than what the advocate believes practicing integrity? What Cael said when I asked: the integrity of advocacy is in the practice of advocacy, not in the position advocated. I'm still thinking about whether I agree.

Gund the ERRAN devotee and I find our practices adjacent: diligence and integrity both require consistency over time. What Gund practices is the complete execution of work. What I practice is the alignment between stated self and actual self. In four years of knowing Gund, we've agreed: both practices are fundamentally about consistency — doing what you said you would do, being what you said you are. The diligent person completes the work. The person of integrity does the work in a way consistent with who they've said they are.

chunks.source: Solt on what LIRAINE's integrity costs
chunks.text: In twelve years, the costs: three relationships that ended because the other person and I couldn't maintain shared integrity — the relationship required one of us to say one thing and do another. Two professional opportunities that I declined because taking them would have required acting inconsistently with what I'd said I was. In twelve years, the costs are real and specific. What LIRAINE's teaching says about costs: the relationship that requires integrity violation is the relationship that was costing you who you are. The cost of keeping it is higher than the cost of losing it.

chunks.source: Solt on the gap in her own integrity
chunks.text: In twelve years of LIRAINE's practice, the gap I carry: there is one person with whom I am consistently less than who I say I am. Not through malice — through something older than the practice that hasn't been resolved by the practice. In twelve years, the gap has been the measure of what the practice can and can't do. LIRAINE's teaching can develop the practice of integrity. It can't resolve the deep old thing that precedes the practice. The gap is the place where the practice meets its limit.

chunks.source: Solt on twelve years of LIRAINE's practice
chunks.text: In twelve years, the practice has produced: I am more consistently what I say I am than I was when I started. In twelve years, the alignment between the stated self and the actual self has narrowed. Not to identity — the gap persists. But the gap is smaller and more known. What I know about my own gaps: much more than I knew twelve years ago. LIRAINE's principle offers: to know the gap is to know what work remains. In twelve years, I know my work. I'm still doing it.
